docs.title: Data Transfer Options, Tips and Solutions
docs.text:
meta

This document is part of the A-LIFE GEMs (Guides, Essentials & Manuals) Collection. This section is part of Manuals -> Yoda -> Transfering data with Cyberduck.

Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier, version 0.2.3, 2025-11-11

docs.title: Cyberduck
docs.text:
When you want to transfer data that has a volume more than 20MB, or more than one data file at once, it is highly recommended to use Cyberduck for accessing Yoda and transfering data from your device. In this document we provide 10 steps to start with Cyberduck.

Please be aware that you need to have access to Yoda via the portal in order to transfer data. If you do not have access to the Yoda portal, please make sure to request storage space [add guide link] or ask permission to the Yoda data project owner to grant you access to the space

docs.title: ✅ 10 Simple Steps for connecting to Yoda with Cyberduck
1. Download Cyberduck Tool
docs.text:
• For Windows users, go to https://cyberduck.io/download/ and download Cyberduck.
  • For MacOS users, there are two options: download it directly from https://cyberduck.io/download/ or search Cyberduck in the VU Software Center Tool and install it in your device. If you do not have VU Software Center Tool you can download it from: https://munki.mac.vu.nl/installers/.

docs.title: 2. Sign in to the Yoda Portal
docs.text:
• Go to: https://portal.yoda.vu.nl
  • Sign in by using your-username@vu.nl and VU password.

docs.title: 3. Generate a new Data Access Password
docs.text:
• Go to: https://portal.yoda.vu.nl/user/data_access
  • Click Generate new data access password
  • For the Label option, type: Cyberduck
  • Click Generate data access password

docs.title: 4. Copy the password
docs.text: • Highlight the generated password and press Command + C to copy.

docs.title: 5. Open Cyberduck and add a new bookmark
docs.text:
• Click the Bookmarks icon of Cyberduck
  • Then click the + button

docs.title: 6. Choose WebDAV (HTTPS) as connection type
docs.text: • Select WebDAV (HTTPS) protocol from the dropdown option list.

docs.title: 7. Fill in the connection details:
docs.text:
• Server: data.yoda.vu.nl
  • Username: your-username@vu.nl
  • Password: paste (Command + v) the password you generated in point 3.

docs.title: 8. Close the bookmark window
docs.text: • Click the X to return to the main Cyberduck home window.

docs.title: 9. Connect to Yoda
docs.text:
• Your new bookmark (data.yoda.vu.nl - WebDAV (HTTPS)) is visible in the home window.
  • Click to the Yoda bookmark to connect and access your Yoda folders.
  • You may need to add your VU password when trying to connect for the first time. Save it for next time.

docs.title: 10. Manage your project directory via the Cyberduck interface
docs.text:
• you can drap and drop files and foleds from your laptop directories to your Yoda project repository.
  • a transfer window keeps open until the full transfer is complete
  • the same operation (from Yoda project directory) to your laptop folders for dragging folders can be repeaded

Warning

Please note that the Data Access Password is valid for 90 days. After that, it expires and you will not be able to login in with Cyberduck. To regain access, simply repeat Steps [3 - 6] for generating a new password and update it in your Cyberduck bookmark.

Info

For more information please take a look at the VU RDM manual - Yoda using Cyberduck

docs.title: Manual — Create an eduID
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Create an eduID manual, part of Manuals in the A-LIFE RDM GEMs collection.

This manual explains how to create an eduID account, which is required to access institutional supported tools, such as Yoda if your institution is not listed in the SRAM institutions list.

  • What is eduID?
  • When should you create an eduID?
  • Steps to create an eduID

Supporting materials: Yoda - Manage Members Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-08-02 — Version: 0.2.0

docs.title: What is eduID?
docs.text:
eduID is a digital identity provided by SURF that gives you a way to log in to websites and other online services in the Netherlands. With your eduID you can access administrative and educational processes at Dutch research and education institutions1 — even if you are not directly affiliated with one. It is designed for users whose institution is not part of the SRAM network, or who have no current institutional affiliation.

We recommend using the eduID app, as it is the most secure and convenient option. The app lets you log in without a password, and two-factor authentication (2FA) provides an extra layer of security.

docs.title: When should you create an eduID?
docs.text:
You need an eduID when you have been invited to a Yoda Research Space but are unable to log in because your institution is not listed among the organisations supported by SRAM.

This is typically the case when:

  • Your institution is not a Dutch research or education organisation
  • Your institution is a Dutch organisation but is not yet connected to SRAM
  • You are an independent researcher or freelancer with no current institutional affiliation

Before creating an eduID, check whether your institution is already supported by SRAM by consulting the list of institutions using SRAM (last accessed: 2026-06-29). If your institution appears in the list, you do not need an eduID — you can log in directly using your institutional credentials.

If your institution is not in the list, or if you try to log in and are redirected to an unfamiliar page without a recognisable login option, then creating an eduID is the recommended solution.

docs.title: Steps to create an eduID
docs.text:
1. Go to the eduID registration page — visit eduid.nl and click Create an eduID.

    Figure 1: Creating an eduID account

  2. Register your account — provide your email address and follow the steps to set up your account, including Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA).

    Use an account you can always access

    Make sure you register your eduID with an email address you can always access. Avoid using an institutional email address from another affiliation, as you may lose access to it in the future (e.g. when leaving an institution). Use a personal email address instead.

Further reading

SRAM invitations and eduID activation — VU Research Support Handbook eduID — SURF IAM documentation eduID support (English)

  1. About eduID: eduid.nl ↩

docs.title: Connect to Research Drive with Cyberduck
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Connect to Research Drive with Cyberduck manual, part of Manuals in the A-LIFE RDM GEMs collection.

This document covers how to connect to your Research Drive project space using Cyberduck via WebDAV and transfer data.

Supporting materials: Transferring Data in Research Drive Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-08-02 — Version: 0.2.0

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Cyberduck is a free desktop client (Windows and macOS) that connects to Research Drive via WebDAV, allowing you to upload, download, and manage your files with a simple drag-and-drop interface.

Before you start

You need to have access to a Research Drive project space before you can transfer data. If you do not have access yet, make sure to first request storage space or ask the Research Drive project owner to grant you access.

For more information on how to get started with Research Drive, see our supportive steps in the Getting Started with Research Drive.

docs.title: Steps for Connecting to Research Drive with Cyberduck
1. Download Cyberduck
docs.text: • Download Cyberduck from https://cyberduck.io/download/ (Windows and macOS).

docs.title: 2. Sign in to Research Drive
docs.text:
• Go to: https://vu.data.surfsara.nl
  • Sign in using your VU credentials.

docs.title: 3. Generate a WebDAV access token
docs.text:
• In Research Drive, open your Personal Settings and navigate to Security (or use this direct link: Security Settings).
Figure 1: Security setting option in the Research Drive main menu.
  • Scroll to App passwords / tokens.

A collection for research data management, including

The guides provide simple steps and context and include examples to make concepts more understanble and familiar. docs.title: Research Data Spotlight — Edition 5
docs.text:
Spotlight on data by

Ecem Yüksel · Systems Biology

Interviewed on 2025-06-27

"One of the most effective habits is to document everything early and consistently, even small decisions like variable naming or code logic."

  • Keywords

    Diet Dietary fiber Fermented food Gut microbiota Microbial diversity

  • Information of Ecem

    • ORCID
    • Yoda
    • Gut Health Enhancement by Eating Favourable Food (GEEFomjebuik)
    • Systems Biology group, A-LIFE
    • Research VU page

docs.title: Can you introduce yourself and tell us which research group you are part of?
docs.text:
My name is Ecem Yüksel, and I'm part of the A-LIFE research group at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, working under the supervision of Remco Kort. I have a background in Biomolecular Sciences, with a focus on cell biology and biological chemistry. Over the years, I've gained research experience in nutrition, particularly exploring the effects of dietary fibers on the human gut microbiome.

My interest in this field began during internships at Keep Food Simple and TNO, in collaboration with the VU. During those experiences, I encountered many passionate scientists whose dedication to nutrition and microbiome research who really inspired me. Nutrition has always excited me, especially when it comes to understanding what is actually healthy and how our dietary choices shape our health.

Throughout my academic journey, I've worked in both wet lab and dry lab environments, which gave me an introduction in data analysis alongside laboratory techniques. This combination has further deepened my interest in pursuing data-driven nutritional research.

docs.title: What is your project about and what kind of data do you work with? How are you generally collecting or generating it?
docs.text:
I'm currently working on a randomized controlled trial (RCT) titled "Distinct modulatory effects of high-fiber and fermented-food diets on gut microbiota, immune function, transit time, and sleep quality in a citizen science randomized controlled trial." The study investigates how different dietary interventions, specifically high-fiber and fermented food diets, affect the gut microbiome, immune responses, transit time, and sleep quality. This project was a true collaborative effort, and I am thankful to have worked alongside esteemed colleagues Maartje van den Belt, Marieke van de Put, Nicole de Wit, and Remco Kort.

The trial includes three groups: a high dietary fiber group (HDF), a high fermented foods group (HFF), and a control group (CG). Data collection occurred over a 5-month period at three time points: baseline (week -1), after the ramp-up phase (week 2), and at the end of the intervention (week 8). Participants were split into two cohorts (n=34 and n=113). The data we collect is multi-dimensional, ranging from microbiome sequencing data, immune markers, and dietary intake records to sleep quality metrics. We primarily employed multivariate analysis to link the observed effects to microbiome composition, with the goal of identifying specific microbial taxa influenced by the dietary interventions.

docs.title: Is your data available for others to access? If yes, where can we find it?
docs.text: Yes, our dataset can be accessed via the VU Yoda environment and can be freely accessed. It is part of a collaborative research project titled: "Distinct modulatory effects of high-fiber and fermented-food diets on gut microbiota, immune function, transit time, and sleep quality in a citizen science randomized controlled trial", Maartje van den Belt, Marieke van de Put, Ecem Yüksel, Nicole de Wit, and Remco Kort, published 1 July 2025. Persistent Identifier (DOI): https://doi.org/10.48338/VU01-K0YFNS. We are proud to make the data openly available so it can support further research in nutrition, gut microbiome science, and personalized health.

docs.title: What is something you wish you had known earlier when it comes to managing research data or collaborating with others?
docs.text: One thing that became clear to me is how important it is to have a clear file structure and consistent naming formats from the start of a project. Since I joined the project in the later stages, I sometimes struggled to locate specific files or understand how data versions were organized.

docs.title: Do you have any practical tips or good habits you would recommend to other A-LIFE researchers who want to manage their data and make it easier to collaborate?
docs.text:
Definitely. One of the most effective habits is to document everything early and consistently, even small decisions like variable naming or code logic. It helps when you or someone else revisits the project months later. Another useful practice is to keep all raw data separate from processed data, with clearly labeled versions so you always know what stage the data is in. And finally, explain where your data lives — having a README that explains where raw data, code, and analysis outputs can be found is incredibly helpful in collaborative environments.

Thank you, Ecem!

Thank you, Ecem, for taking the time to share your work with us. It was great to hear about your project, and your tips on managing data will be really helpful for other researchers.

docs.title: Research Data Spotlight — Edition 2
docs.text:
Spotlight on data by

Judith Smit · Sensory Ecology & Evolution

Interviewed on 2025-02-17

"Providing clear annotations in your code and creating a good README file make your work more understandable for others and you'll benefit from it yourself."

  • Keywords

    Behavioural Ecology Sexual communication Noise pollution Light pollution Engystomops pustulosus Túngara frog Dataverse Dryad

  • Information of Judith

    • ORCID
    • Dryad dataset
    • Dataverse data
    • Zenodo Repository
    • Ecology & Evolution Group, A-LIFE
    • Research VU page
    • judithsmit.bsky.social

docs.title: Could you briefly introduce yourself? What has your academic journey been like so far, and which research group are you currently part of?
docs.text: I am very interested in why animals do what they do, and specifically how their communication systems work. I love designing and conducting experiments on animal behaviour! After obtaining my BSc and MSc on animal behavior at Utrecht University, I started my PhD at the VU. I investigated the effects of urbanization on sexual communication in túngara frogs, and obtained my PhD in October 2024. I'm very excited to start my postdoc at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama in 2025, during which I will investigate communication in treehoppers.

docs.title: Can you tell us about a specific dataset from your research? Why is it significant to your project, and what makes it particularly important?
docs.text:
In October 2024 we published an article in Behavioral Ecology titled "Urban sensory conditions alter rival interactions and mate choice in urban and forest túngara frogs", which was the last chapter of my PhD dissertation. In this project we conducted behavioural experiments to test how light and noise pollution affect rival interactions and mate choice. We collected many different data sets, and we need to write a long code to merge data sets and to run statistical models and simulations. When we first submitted the paper to a journal in January 2024, we decided to publish a pre-print in BioRXiv together with the data sheets and the R code. This preprint was downloaded more than 300 times before the final manuscript was published in a scientific journal. Doing science (from conceiving the idea to publishing the manuscript) usually takes several years, and by publishing preprints this process can hopefully be sped up.

To me, open science is very important for two main reasons. First, it provides transparency, for instance during the review process. Although reviewers are often limited in their time, I believe reviewing the data sheets and code could improve the quality of science. Second, by sharing data and code other researchers could benefit, for example by using similar analyses. It could benefit science overall if people did not have to keep inventing the wheel over and over again. I hope we are moving into the direction in which sharing data and code will be mandatory when submitting a manuscript.

docs.title: Have you used any storage tools or any data management solutions provided by the VU? What feature of the solution do you think has been for you the most useful for your research workflow?
docs.text: I had very helpful advice from VU where I could share my data and code at the pre-print stage. Also, the A-LIFE RDM team shared with me a template for making a README file, which was very helpful for me as well! When the journal required me to upload the data to Dryad, it was very easy to modify my README file to fit the specific template of this repository.

docs.title: Is your dataset available for others to access? If so, where can we find it? Are there any related works linked to it? If yes, how did you go about linking the sources?
docs.text: Yes, the data and the code are openly available. Data via Dryad, and the code via Zenodo. With the preprint I used DataVerse to upload the data and the code. Upon acceptance of the manuscript, the journal required us to upload the data via Dryad, and it was possible to add a link to Zenodo for the R code. For Dryad there was a specific format for the README file, which included a section with general information such as the time and location of data collection and language used in the field. Besides, each column header in the data sheets required a description and unit. Fortunately, I had already worked on making a clear README file before and modifying it for Dryad was pretty easy!

docs.title: Looking back at your experience managing this dataset, what tips would you give to researchers for organising and managing their data more effectively? What helped you avoid data chaos?
docs.text:
I would advise others to consider publishing a pre-print, the code and data sheets in an early stage in the publication process. For this, it is important to provide clear annotations in the code for others to understand it and to create a README file for the data set to make it understandable for others. If I am working on data sets and code with the plan of sharing, it definitely forces me to make my work more clear and readable (which I am benefitting from myself as well ).

Thank you, Judith!

Thank you, Judith, for sharing your fascinating research and also for sharing thoughtful tips on data management — good luck with your new adventure in Panama!

docs.title: Research Data Spotlight — Edition 4
docs.text:
Spotlight on data by

Julia Beets · Ecology & Evolution

Interviewed on 2025-05-06

"If you incorporate the goal of accessible data in your workflow early on, the process won't take much extra time near publication."

  • Keywords

    Drosophila melanogaster Life-history traits Single nucleotide polymorphisms Genetic variation Functional genomics Bioinformatics SciStor

  • Information of Julia

    • ORCID

    • GitHub - FlyCADD tool
    • Manuscript preprint
    • Journal article
    • Ecology & Evolution group, A-LIFE
    • Research VU page

docs.title: Can you tell us a bit about yourself and what your research is about?
docs.text: With a master's degree in Biomolecular sciences, I am currently working as a PhD student in the Ecology & Evolution section of A-LIFE. My research focuses on the impact of genetic variation on life-history traits of the Drosophila melanogaster, the fruit fly. More specifically, I am interested in the impact of single nucleotide variations and to study this, I work both on bioinformatics and data, as well as functional genomics in the lab.

docs.title: How do you keep track of your data? Do you collaborate with others?
docs.text:
My main strategy is to start early with documentation and data storage structures. I keep a descriptive file throughout the research process, which can easily be translated into a documentation file for data sharing purposes. For code, it is very important to properly annotate the scripts.

In collaborations, I like to work in the same document with track changes or comments, so all contributors have equal opportunities to read and edit, and regular backups of this document for version control. My data is currently in SciStor, with access provided to most collaborators via the BAZIS HPC Cluster.

docs.title: Is your data accessible? If yes, where can we find it? What was the most challenging part of sharing your data?
docs.text:
Yes, the data is accessible. For my most recent project, I developed a tool, FlyCADD, to score the impact of any single nucleotide variant in the fruit fly genome based on the CADD framework applied to the human genome. The data (both the data required for development, as well as the data generated by the tool) is available on Zenodo, and is linked with the code on GitHub.

Deciding where to share the data and code was challenging, as there are many options for repositories. These repositories differed in regard to data requirements, storage space, integration with other repositories, preprint requirements and licencing, for example. Our data consisted of different data types, and code for the prediction tool, and additionally the manuscript was preprinted. We picked Zenodo as data repository as it has the possibility of linking a GitHub repository with the tool, applying version control and an intuitive upload interface.

docs.title: If a colleague asked you for some advice about managing their data, what would you suggest?
docs.text: Keep your files organized and keep track of any updates, changes or important parameters. Being able to quickly retrieve any information, whether it is data or metadata, will make your workflow easier to execute, and will be a preparation for a smooth conversion of all (meta)data into a format suitable for publishing, as all information will already be written up.

docs.title: Journals more often ask for data to be accessible. Does that just feel like extra work, or do you think it makes sense nowadays and you would share it anyways?
docs.text:
It is some extra work to make data accessible when the journal requires this. However, it does make your article more accessible, reproducible and interesting for readers. Sharing all data that was used in the article helps other researchers to build further on similar topics. If you incorporate the goal of accessible data in your workflow early on, the process won't take much extra time near publication.

Thank you, Julia!

Thank you, Julia, for sharing your fascinating research and also for sharing thoughtful tips on data management and collaboration — a great inspiration for anyone working with data!

docs.text:
Spotlight on data by

Niek Barmentlo · Ecology & Evolution

Interviewed on 2024-10-28

"I didn't expect to care about FAIR, but it is surprisingly fun and helps me structure my thoughts and project."

  • Keywords

    Ecology Genomics DNA sequencing African Swine Fever Wild Boars Yoda

  • Information of Niek

    • ORCID
    • Yoda dataset
    • GitHub Repository
    • Ecology and Evolution Group
    • Research VU page

docs.title: Can you introduce yourself and tell us which research group you are part of?
docs.text: I am part of the Ecology & Evolution section, in particular the Evolution group. It is a fairly broad group, but we all tend to use evolutionary theory to explain ecological observations in either controlled or wild settings.

docs.title: Can you briefly explain your research and what inspired you to work in this area?
docs.text:
My project investigates the paradoxical resistance of certain free-living wild boar to the disease caused by African Swine Fever Virus. This pathogen was thought, and observed in controlled situations, to cause 100% lethality in wild boars. However, in wild situations, researchers have observed surviving boar. The question is now what is different between these groups?

I use a combination of genomics, transcriptomics and microbiomics to tackle this question. For me, this research is incredibly exciting as it combines conservation and evolutionary research, implying that I have the "huh, how does this work, evolutionary-speaking?" moments while helping guide conservation efforts!

docs.title: Have you made your data available yet? If so, where can we find it?
docs.text: Most of my data is currently not downloadable, but all metadata has been written down. For storage purposes, I tend to use Yoda, it is easy enough to use, and allows for both active storage of extra sensitive data as well as 'cheap' archiving of data. Specifically, the archiving is great! When dealing with genomics, one often times only needs the "raw data" for the first step of the bioinformatics pipeline. For me, this means that I require a method to store raw data in an environment that is not my expensive supercomputer storage, and this is where Yoda shines! Additionally, the metadata files needed to be added in Yoda make sure that you can easily match your data to a paper and your code in e.g. a GitHub repository. An example of a small public dataset of mine can be found in Yoda.

docs.title: What has been the most beneficial aspect of applying data management best practices? Has applying these practices changed the way you approach your research?
docs.text: Genomics datasets are huge! One of my current experiments deals with about 2 terabytes of data, which is sometimes a hassle to keep track of. Especially when you are sequencing samples with companies, you really need to know where your samples came from and what kind of quality and dataset size you can expect from sequencing. Recently, I did a DNA sequencing job with a company in two successions; the first round was to understand how much of the isolated DNA was non-host and the second run was to sequence eligible samples with less contamination in higher quality. The sequencing company messed up the amount of gigabases I wanted per sample, which I only figured out because I knew for each sample what the likely output was supposed to be. All that data management information is stored in large Excels with sufficient README files to keep track of them.

docs.title: If your data could speak, what advice do you think it would give to other researchers trying to manage their own datasets?
docs.text:
In genomics, the data produced is maybe as important as the results produced. If my data could speak, it would say that I should make sure that it is clearly described so it can be used in future studies. As sequencing is expensive, the scientific community should deem it her duty to make sure that labs with less funds can also use genomics data and make sure that scientist don't unnecessarily produce data when it is already available online.

Thank you, Niek!

Thank you, Niek, for sharing your fascinating research and also for sharing thoughtful tips on data management — good luck with your project!

docs.title: Research Data Spotlight — Edition 3
docs.text:
Spotlight on data by

Simone van de Zande · Systems Biology

Interviewed on 2025-03-11

"Good communication, clear documentation and a well organised data structure make collaboration and sharing much easier."

  • Keywords

    Experimental evolution Imaging data Sequencing data Microbial physiology Adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE)

  • Information of Simone

    • ORCID
    • EVOGOLD
    • Evoducta
    • Systems Biology Lab
    • Systems Biology section, A-LIFE
    • Research VU page

docs.title: Can you tell us a bit about yourself and which part of your research group you are part of?
docs.text: I am someone who likes to do a bit of everything. I obtained two BSc degrees, one in Biomedical Sciences (UM) and one in Business analytics (VU) and combined these skills in a MSc in Bioinformatics and Systems Biology with a double major (VU). I am now part of the Systems Biology Lab as a PhD student working on the EVOGOLD project in which my colleagues and I are developing a new adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) method and auxiliary device. There are many unknowns in this project, and I particularly enjoy the multidisciplinary approach — we tackle microbiology while also designing our own bioprocess, considering factors like fluid dynamics.

docs.title: What is your research project about, and what kind of data do you work with?
docs.text: The EVOGOLD project focuses on developing a new method for experimental evolution. As we are working with a novel device, which is still under development, the project involves a lot of characterization of growth within this new system. To achieve this, we built a custom imaging setup to track microbial behaviour and then we use custom python scripts for analysing high-quality time-series imaging data. Additionally, since the goal of this new method is to elicit (beneficial) mutations, a lot of whole genome sequencing data is collected as well as phenotypical data of these strains. We carefully catalogue these strains and their properties to establish links between the grown strains, their mutations, and growing conditions.

docs.title: What challenges have you faced in managing your research data so far?
docs.text: The challenging part was to maintain an overview and transparency in our data since we are creating a large collective database. We have had to have good discussions about our strategies and luckily the RDM team helped us with creating a complete list of variables that we should keep track of to make our data comply with FAIR principles.

docs.title: How do you collaborate and manage your project with other contributors? What strategies have helped make collaboration easier for you?
docs.text:
We keep our experiments in shared folders, along with a file describing results and locations for easy comparison and retrieval. We have also created a uniform file naming structure and corresponding abbreviation list that not only facilitates the file system, but also enables us to easily identify contents from the file and folder name.

For managing microbial strains, we use an excel file with templated layout which is shared throughout the PI's group in OneDrive such that it can periodically be updated into one collective file. The layout incorporates standard identifiers, such as GenBank IDs and NCBI taxonomy IDs.

For our Python scripts developed for analysing the images we maintain a shared repository with version history and a log of changes and dependencies.

docs.title: Based on your experience so far, what is one data organisation/tool tip that has made your life easier and that you think other A-LIFE researchers should know?
docs.text:
I do not rely on specific tools to recommend, but I believe good communication and establishing clear agreements with collaborators are crucial, as everyone has their own logic and approach to data management. Creating a consistent structure for documenting and storing data, along with clear descriptions, helps facilitate data sharing not only within the team but also for others who may need access later.

Thank you, Simone!

Thank you, Simone, for sharing your fascinating research and also for sharing thoughtful tips on data management — success with this fascinating project!

docs.title: Research Data Spotlight — Edition 6
docs.text:
Spotlight on data by

Wouter van der Vegt · Ecology & Evolution

Interviewed on 2026-06-24

"It is our responsibility as scientists to show colleagues, stakeholders, and ultimately the wider public how we arrived at our conclusions."

  • Keywords

    Trait Soil fauna Urban biodiversity Open data Community ecology Ground beetles Yoda

  • Information of Wouter

    • ORCID
    • GitHub
    • Manuscript preprint
    • Yoda data
    • Ecology & Evolution group, A-LIFE
    • Research VU page

docs.title: Can you introduce yourself and tell us which research group you are part of?
docs.text: My name is Wouter van der Vegt and I am a PhD candidate in the Ecology & Evolution section. I started my adventure here at the VU almost ten years ago as a biology bachelor student and over time became more and more fascinated by small critters such as spiders, isopods, springtails (if you don't know them, Google them; they are cool), and beetles. Thus, it was an obvious choice to pursue an internship steeped in ecology. Little did I know that this was the first spark that led me to study the creatures that live right beneath our feet in cities.

docs.title: What is your research project about, and what kind of data do you work with? How do you typically collect or generate it?
docs.text:
I work on the biodiversity and traits of fauna in urban environments. More specifically, I am unravelling hidden biodiversity by examining those often overlooked, namely soil fauna. Although many (soil) species suffer from human impacts, some do not, and others even flourish in human-dominated ecosystems. That's where the traits come in. By looking at which traits the animals have in cities, and which traits they have outside of cities, we can infer what kind of 'trait package' these animal communities need to 'do well' in cities. Other similar green spaces that haven't been investigated or are still being built (but are designed to look similar) are then expected to host animals with similar traits.

The animals, in my research mainly ground beetles, are collected via pitfall traps (small buckets placed into the soil, with the opening at surface level) placed in urban green spaces — this has led to multiple weird gazes or people highly intrigued by what 'that guy' [me] was doing in the bushes. After placing the traps, we wait a few days and come back to collect them. In the lab, we identify the species, measure traits such as heat tolerance and walking behaviour, and complement these with traits previously described in the literature. So there is enough diversity in my work and the species that I work with.

docs.title: Are there any RDM tools or practices you use, whether provided by the VU or not, to store, document, or organise your data?
docs.text: I had good chats with both data stewards about how to store and archive my data. I work day-to-day in Google Drive, but our conversations made it clear that YODA was the place to store and archive the relevant data and scripts associated with the manuscript I was about to submit. I started with a README template from a colleague (who originally had received this from RDM team and adapted it to their liking). I edited and tweaked it to fit my project and before long everything was done, documented and FAIR.

docs.title: Is your data accessible to others? If so, where can we find it? Are there any related outputs linked to it, such as code, publications, or a preprint?
docs.text: Absolutely! The more, the merrier. That applies to both open data and people. It can be retrieved, along with the scripts, on YODA. The preprint is accessible here.

docs.title: Now that your data is publicly available, what do you think the biggest benefit will be for yourself, for your field, or for others?
docs.text:
Although it would be nice if my data were cited, that is not really my motivation. To me, it simply feels like the right thing to do. At conferences, I've heard PIs say they can no longer make sense of their datasets from a few years ago and laugh about it (let alone that someone else will be able to understand it…). I get that it is extra work to properly document and annotate, and in some cases, privacy concerns can complicate it and needs to be handled carefully. However, I'd say it is our responsibility as scientists to show colleagues, stakeholders, and ultimately the wider public how we arrived at our conclusions.

There is also a practical benefit. Finding a well-documented dataset and script that does what you want to do with your data can save a huge amount of time. There is no need to re-invent the wheel if this is openly available (and actually works!). As long as you understand what it is doing and verify that it works not only for the original data, but also for your own analyses, everyone benefits ;).

Thank you, Wouter!

Thank you, Wouter, for sharing your data journey and your inspiring reminder that a well-documented dataset and script can save everyone from re-inventing the wheel!

docs.title: What is a Research Tool?
docs.text:
According to SURF, a research tool is a service that supports one or more stages of the research lifecycle — from data collection and processing to analysis, collaboration, publication, and preservation.1

Storage is one of the most fundamental components of research data management: it determines where your data lives while you are working on it, how it is shared with collaborators, and ultimately where it will be safely preserved at the end of your project. Not all storage is the same: active storage is where your data is created and used day-to-day, while archive storage is where your finalised data is deposited for the long term and made findable and reusable through a persistent identifier such as a DOI.

Alongside storage, there are tools that help you move data around — between your computer and a storage platform, between collaborators, or from one system to another. These transfer tools are not storage solutions themselves, but they are an essential part of getting your data where it needs to be, safely and efficiently.

In this documentation we currently focus on the tools supported at the VU, and we hope to expand coverage in the future. We also include other tools that are widely used in the A-LIFE environment and are accepted, secure, and well-established in the research community.

docs.title: Tool Classification in this RDM Collection

The table below gives an overview of the tools covered in this documentation, their category, and whether they are officially supported at the VU. VU Supported ✅ means the tool is listed on the VU Storage Finder.

  • Archive Storage (Archiving & Publishing) — platforms for depositing finalised datasets for long-term preservation and making them publicly available with a persistent identifier such as a DOI. Unlike active storage, these are not designed for working files.
  • Transfer — tools for moving data between your local machine and a storage or archiving platform, or for sending large files securely to collaborators. They are not storage solutions themselves — they are the means by which you get data in and out of them.

docs.title: Cyberduck
docs.text:
When you want to transfer data that has a volume more than 20MB, or more than one data file at once, it is highly recommended to use Cyberduck for accessing Yoda and transfering data from your device. In this document we provide 10 steps to start with Cyberduck.

Please note that you need to have access to Yoda via the portal in order to transfer data. The following steps are for MacOS users.

:::success

✅ 10 Simple Steps for connecting to Yoda with Cyberduck

1. Download the VU Software Center Tool → Go to: https://munki.mac.vu.nl/installers/

2. In the VU Software Center Tool, search for Cyberduck and install it in your device.

3. Sign in to the Yoda Portal → Go to: https://portal.yoda.vu.nl. → Sign in by using your-username@vu.nl and VU password.

4. Generate a new Data Access Password → Go to: https://portal.yoda.vu.nl/user/data_access → Click Generate new data access password → For the Label, type: Cyberduck → Click Generate data access password

5. Copy the password → Highlight the generated password and press Command + C to copy.

6. Open Cyberduck and add a new bookmark → Click the Bookmarks icon → Then click the + button

7. Choose WebDAV (HTTPS) as connection type → Select WebDAV (HTTPS) protocol from the dropdown list.

8. Fill in the connection details: - Server: data.yoda.vu.nl - Username: your-username@vu.nl - Password: paste (Command + v) the password you generated in point 4.

9. Close the bookmark window → Click the X to return to the main Cyberduck home window.

10. Connect to Yoda → Your new bookmark (data.yoda.vu.nl - WebDAV (HTTPS)) is visible in the home window. → Click to the Yoda bookmark to connect and access your Yoda folders. → You may need to add your VU password when trying to connect for the first time. Save it for next time.

:::

:::warning Please note that the Data Access Password is valid for ==90== days. After that, it expires and you will not be able to login in with Cyberduck. To regain access, simply repeat Steps [4 - 7] to create a new password and update it in your Cyberduck bookmark. :::

:::info For more information please take a look at the VU RDM manual -Yoda using Cyberduck :::

docs.title: What is Cyberduck?
docs.text:
Cyberduck is a free, open-source tool for connecting to your research storage — such as Yoda and Research Drive — from your own computer. Once connected, it works like a regular folder: drag and drop files to upload or download, no command line needed. It supports WebDAV, SFTP, S3, and other protocols, making it a flexible option for transferring data between your local machine and your research storage space.

Download Cyberduck for your device for free here:

Download Cyberduck

docs.title: Why use Cyberduck?
docs.text:
• Free and open-source — no cost, available for both Mac and Windows.
  • Simple drag-and-drop interface — works like a regular folder on your device, no command line needed.
  • Checksum verification — confirms that a file arrived intact and wasn't corrupted during transfer, especially useful for large research datasets.
  • Bookmarks — save your storage connections for quick, repeated access; the same bookmark file works on both Mac and Windows.
  • Multi-protocol support — connects via WebDAV, SFTP, S3, and more, so it works with Yoda, Research Drive, and other storage platforms.

docs.title: What is SURFfilesender?
docs.text: SURFfilesender is a secure file transfer service provided by SURF1 that allows you to share large files easily and securely. The recipient does not need an account to download files — they simply receive a link and can access the data directly. This makes it ideal for sharing data with external collaborators, reviewers, or anyone outside your institution. It is available to all VU affiliated staff and students.

docs.title: How to use SURFfilesender
docs.text:
For step-by-step instructions on how to transfer data with SURFfilesender, see the dedicated manual:

Transfer data with SURFfilesender

docs.title: Why use SURFfilesender?
docs.text:
• Share files up to 1 TB in size
  • Works via your web browser — no software or plugins needed
  • Recipient does not need an account
  • Two sharing options: by email or via an anonymous link
  • End-to-end encryption available for extra security
  • Links are valid for a defined period of time, with a maximum of 30 days
  • Files are stored in the Netherlands

docs.title: When to use SURFfilesender?
docs.text:
SURFfilesender is a good option in situations such as:

  • Anonymous link — you need to share data without revealing who is sending it, for example during double-blind peer review
  • For review — you are in the review process before publication and your data is not yet publicly available
  • Your DOI is not yet created or not yet resolving — your dataset may not yet be archived or published, or the DOI exists but is temporarily not resolving due to a technical issue; SURFfilesender provides a secure temporary alternative while waiting for the issue to be fixed
  • The recipient has no account on Research Drive or Yoda — and creating one is not practical for a one-off transfer
  • You need to transfer a large file quickly — without setting up a shared folder or storage space

Check your data sharing conditions

Check your data sharing conditions before sending. If you are not sure, contact your A-LIFE team to see how to proceed.

docs.title: What is Zenodo?
docs.text:
Zenodo is a free and open digital archive built by CERN2 and OpenAIRE, enabling researchers to share and preserve research outputs of any size, format, and from all fields of research.1 Launched in May 2013, it was originally developed to support the European Commission's Open Data policy as a catch-all repository for EC-funded research.

Zenodo accepts a wide range of research outputs:

  • Datasets — tabular data, observational data, experimental results
  • Software — code, scripts, analysis pipelines, specific repository versions
  • Publications — preprints, reports, theses
  • Presentations and posters — conference materials
  • Other — images, videos, interactive notebooks, and more

Zenodo imposes no requirements on format, size, access restrictions, or licence — removing barriers to sharing for researchers in any discipline. Every record receives a DOI, and metadata is automatically registered with DataCite and integrated into OpenAIRE reporting lines to funding agencies.

According to the VU Research Data and Software Management Policy, all research data and software that lead to published results must be archived and published in a trusted repository. Beyond policy compliance, publishing research data increases transparency, reproducibility, and the visibility and impact of your work.

Did you know?

Zenodo is derived from Zenodotus, the first librarian of the Library of Alexandria and father of the first recorded use of metadata

docs.title: Why use Zenodo?
docs.text:
• Free — no cost for uploading datasets up to 50 GB; multiple datasets can be uploaded with no size limit on communities.
  • Easy to use — intuitive interface with drag-and-drop file upload.
  • Accepts many formats — datasets, software, publications, posters, presentations, images, videos, and interactive materials.
  • DOI — every published record receives a DOI, making your data citable and findable.
  • Long-term preservation — data is stored in the trusted CERN data centre.
  • Increases visibility — widely known in the research community; data is searchable worldwide.
  • Complies with funder requirements — trusted by many funders and publishers as a reliable repository.
  • Supports open science — promotes transparency and reusability; supported by OpenAIRE.
  • Versioning — datasets can be updated as new versions.
  • GitHub integration — synchronise with a GitHub repository to preserve specific versions of your work.

Basic Information

docs.title: Digital Object Identifier — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Reserve a DOI before publishing by clicking Get a DOI now! — the DOI is registered only when the record is published.
  • If you select Yes, do not provide a DOI linked to a journal article. Instead, add the article DOI in the Related works field.

docs.text:
• Provide a title that reflects the content of the data. The title is used in citations and for discovery.
  • Keep it concise. Use Add additional title/subtitle for very long titles.
  • A good format for datasets: "Dataset for [Title of your article]"
  • Avoid special characters (e.g. # % & @).

docs.title: Publication Date — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Defaults to the date the draft was created. Can be modified.
  • Use ISO format: YYYY-MM-DD.

docs.title: Creator — Mandatory
docs.text:
• A Creator is an author of the dataset and is included in the citation.
  • Search by ORCID to auto-populate name and affiliation.
  • It is highly recommended to provide an ORCID and a ROR affiliation for each Creator. The affiliation field is auto-completed from the ROR database.

docs.title: Description — Mandatory
docs.text:
• Provide a paragraph or short summary describing your dataset — it appears under the title once published.
  • Do not copy the abstract of your article — the Description should specifically describe the dataset.
  • The Description is not a substitute for a README file: the Description gives a general summary; the README describes the content of individual files.

A good example

See a good Description example from an A-LIFE researcher: Zenodo dataset.

docs.title: Licence — Mandatory
docs.text:
• A licence is required for others to reuse your data. By default, CC BY 4.0 is applied.
  • For datasets, see How do I licence my research data?.
  • For software, see Choose a Licence.
  • For an overview of common licences, see our GEMs — Licences page.

docs.title: Copyright — Recommended
docs.text: • A copyright statement describing ownership of the uploaded resource. By default: Copyright © (2025) The Authors.

docs.title: 2. Recommended Information
docs.text:
Recommended Information

Definition: Not strictly required to publish, but highly recommended for a complete and well-documented record. Type: Recommended

docs.title: Contributors — Optional
docs.text:
• Add Contributors in the same way as Creators — they are not included in the citation.
  • Do not add a person as a Contributor if they are already listed as a Creator.
  • Assign a Role (e.g. Supervisor, Contact person, Sponsor) — equivalent to someone you would include in manuscript Acknowledgements.

docs.title: Keywords and Subjects — Optional but highly recommended
docs.text:
• Keywords are free-form text; Subjects are from controlled vocabularies (e.g. Medical Subject Headings — MeSH).
  • Press Enter or click Add after each term to create separate tags — do not enter all terms as one string.
  • Check if your term is already in the European Science Vocabulary (EuroSciVoc) — shown as EuroSciVoc in the dropdown.
Selecting keywords and subjects from standard vocabularies

docs.title: Languages — Optional
docs.text: • More than one language can be selected.

docs.title: Dates — Optional
docs.text:
• Add specific date types beyond the publication date (e.g. submission or acceptance dates for preprints).
  • Use ISO format: YYYY-MM-DD.

docs.title: Version — Recommended
docs.text:
• For a first publication, use 1.0.0.
  • Increment the version number for each subsequent update (e.g. 1.1.0 follows 1.0.0).

Semantic versioning

See Introduction to semantic versioning for guidance on versioning datasets and software.

docs.title: Publisher — Optional
docs.text: • The Publisher appears in the citation. Zenodo is the default and will be visible in your record's citation. You may replace it with your institution's name.

docs.title: 3. Other Information
docs.text:
Other Information

Definition: Additional contextual information. Not mandatory, but recommended if the information exists. Type: Optional

docs.title: Funding — Optional but recommended
docs.text:
• Provide funding information for awards and grants associated with your research.
  • Standard award/grant: click + Add.
  • Custom award/grant: click + Add Custom — the funder must be registered in ROR.
  • More than one funding source can be added.

docs.title: Related works — Optional but highly recommended
docs.text:
• Use this field to cross-link your dataset with related publications, datasets, or other resources.
  • Mandatory sub-fields: Relation type, Identifier, and Scheme.
  • The most common relation type for datasets is Is Supplement To (links your dataset to a related article).
  • See the full list of DataCite Relation Types.

docs.title: References — Optional
docs.text: • Prefer using Related works to cross-link resources rather than this field.

docs.title: Software — Optional
docs.text:
• Relevant for Software resource types. Sub-fields: Repository URL, Programming language, and Repository status (e.g. Active).

Using GitHub with Zenodo?

Zenodo integrates with GitHub to automatically archive repository versions. See Referencing content on GitHub and Zenodo GitHub and Software.

docs.title: Publishing information — Optional
docs.text: • Relevant for manuscripts uploaded to Zenodo. Fields include Journal, Book, etc.

docs.title: Conference — Optional
docs.text: • Relevant for conference-related outputs (posters, presentations). Include the conference name and location.

docs.title: Domain specific fields — Optional
docs.text:
• Include domain-specific metadata where applicable.

What next?

Metadata complete! Continue to Step 3 — Publishing in Zenodo to run pre-publishing checks and submit your record.

  1. GitHub Docs — Referencing and citing content: https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/archiving-a-github-repository/referencing-and-citing-content ↩

  2. Zenodo Documentation — GitHub and Software: https://help.zenodo.org/docs/github/ ↩

docs.title: Metadata and Documenting Data in Zenodo
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Metadata and Documenting Data in Zenodo page, part of Other Tools → Zenodo in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

Before publishing in Zenodo, good documentation makes your dataset findable, citable, and reusable. This page covers:

  • Metadata and README
  • Completing the Metadata Form
  • Documenting your data

Supporting materials: Best Practices — Filling in the Metadata Form, Essentials — README Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-08-02 — Version: 0.2.0

docs.title: Metadata and README
docs.text:
A well-documented Zenodo package has two complementary layers:

  • Metadata — structured fields (title, creators, description, licence, resource type, etc.) that you fill in directly in the Zenodo interface when creating a record. Metadata is machine-readable, feeds search engines and data catalogues, and makes your dataset findable and citable. Some fields are mandatory; others are strongly recommended.
  • README — a plain text file that you write and include inside your uploaded files (or ZIP archive). It is human-readable and describes the content of the files, how the data was collected, and how to use it. The README is not enforced by Zenodo, but it is strongly recommended and required by the A-LIFE checklist before archiving.

Metadata answers "what is this dataset?" for search engines and catalogues. The README answers "what is in these files?" for the person who downloads them.

docs.title: Completing the Metadata Form
docs.text:
When you create a new upload in Zenodo, you fill in a metadata form as part of the archiving process. The form includes three categories of fields: Basic (mandatory), Recommended, and Other (optional).

Key things to prepare in advance:

  • Title — a clear, descriptive title for the dataset (not just "data")
  • Creators — names, affiliations, and ORCID identifiers for all contributors
  • Description — a concise summary of what the dataset contains and what research it supports; you can copy the key content from your README
  • Resource type — choose the type that best fits (dataset, software, poster, etc.)
  • Licence — decide which licence applies to your data before uploading; check with your data steward if unsure
  • Related publications — link your dataset to any associated article using its DOI

For step-by-step guidance on every field in the Zenodo metadata form, follow our dedicated best practice guide:

Best Practices — Completing the Zenodo Metadata Form

docs.title: Documenting your data
docs.text: We explicitly recommend including a README file in your Zenodo package before submitting for publication. A README is a plain text file (.md or .txt) that describes the content of your dataset. Include it inside your ZIP archive or upload it as a separate file alongside your data files.

docs.title: What to include in your README
docs.text:
A good Zenodo README should cover:

  • A short description of the dataset and what research question or publication it supports
  • A list of the files or folders included, with a brief description of each
  • Information about how the data was collected, generated, or processed
  • Software, tools, or dependencies needed to open or work with the files
  • Licence information
  • Contact details

Tip

Copy the key description from your README into the Zenodo Description field when filling in the metadata form — this ensures the content is visible on the dataset landing page without requiring a download.

README template and tips

See the README section in our GEMs for a ready-to-use template and examples.

Get inspired by your A-LIFE colleagues!

Not sure where to start? A great way to get inspired is to look at what your A-LIFE colleagues have done! The datasets below are published by A-LIFE researchers and archived in Zenodo — each includes a README you can browse directly on the record page. Take a look at how they described their files and structured their documentation. Every research domain is different, so feel free to adapt what you see to your own workflow.

Model output and scripts for QUINCY-JSM simulations for Amazonian forest sites — Fleischer, Katrin et al. (2026) · DOI · View README

Data and code for "Predicting the functional impact of single nucleotide variants in Drosophila melanogaster with FlyCADD" — Beets, Julia et al. (2025) · DOI · View README

What next?

Metadata prepared and README ready? Continue to Publishing in Zenodo to publish.

docs.title: Organise your Data
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Organise your Data page, part of Other Tools → Zenodo in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

This page provides guidance on how to prepare and organise your data before archiving in Zenodo:

  • How Zenodo organises data
  • Organise before transferring data in Zenodo

Supporting materials: Best Practices — Organising Data, FAQs Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-08-02 — Version: 0.2.0

docs.title: How Zenodo organises data
docs.text:
In Zenodo, each record corresponds to one published dataset. A record contains:

  • The data files you upload (individual files or a ZIP archive)
  • The metadata describing your dataset (title, creators, description, licence, etc.)
  • A README file — highly recommended; describes the content of your uploaded files, included inside your ZIP or as a separate file
  • A DOI assigned at the time of publication

Unlike a shared drive or folder structure, Zenodo does not have a nested folder hierarchy — each record is a flat collection of files under a single DOI. If you want to publish separate datasets (e.g. two experiments), you create two separate records.

docs.title: Organise before transferring data in Zenodo
docs.text:
Once a record is published in Zenodo, not everything can be changed in the same way:

  • Metadata (title, creators, description, licence, etc.) — can be edited directly at any time, without creating a new version.
  • Data files (adding, removing, or modifying files) — requires creating a new version of the record. Each new version gets its own DOI, which is automatically linked to all previous versions — so existing citations still work. But ideally, you want to get it right the first time.

Taking a few minutes to organise your data before uploading will save you from having to republish. Good organisation also ensures that:

  • Others can understand and reuse your data without needing to contact you
  • Your dataset complies with FAIR data principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable)
  • Your metadata accurately describes what is in the files

Follow our general guide for support on directory structure, file naming and file versioning. It applies to any tool or device, not just for Zenodo publication.

Best Practices — Organising data

What next?

Data organised and ready? Continue to Transferring Data to upload your files to Zenodo.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Publishing page, part of Other Tools → Zenodo in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

This document covers the final steps before publishing your dataset in Zenodo:

  • Pre-publishing checks
  • How to publish your data in Zenodo

Authors: Irene Martorelli, Brett Olivier — Last modification: 2026-08-02 — Version: 0.6.0

docs.title: 1. Pre-publishing checks
docs.text:
Complete these checks before submitting for publication

We strongly recommend going through each check below before publishing — it helps you catch errors and ensures your dataset meets quality standards.

docs.title: 1a. Draft Preview
docs.text:
Before publishing the dataset, it is highly recommended to select the Preview option of the draft. It is on the side right side bar of the interface.

Figure 1: Draft preview option.

In the Preview option, you are able to view how the record will look like once it is published. This is always highly recommended to do as you will be able to also spot errors.

Figure 2: Preview display record view.

docs.title: 1b. Share Access
docs.text:
Zenodo also provides the possibility to Share your draft with others before submitting.

Figure 3: Share the data record.

It is possible to add Zenodo users and invite people by sending an invitation.

Figure 4: Add a member.

This is useful for collaborating in the same draft before submitting and checking with your collaborators if everything provided is correct. It is requested to provide the type of Access for the new person added.

Figure 5: Manage user accessibility.

docs.title: 1c. Visibility
docs.text:
Zenodo provides only two options for data Accessibility: Open and Restricted.

  • Open allows all the metadata and all the data published to be public, thus visible and accessible to everyone. This includes also the option to download the data files.
Figure 6: Open accessibility.
  • For the Restricted option, only the metadta information will be visible while the data files can only be accessed by users specified in the permissions.
Figure 7: Restricted option.

docs.title: 1d. Community
docs.text:
Zenodo provides the possibility to submit the dataset to a Community. This option can be done by "Select a Community"option.

Figure 8: Select a community option.

There is then a selection of communities that you can pick from. Submit your dataset record for inclusion in a Community from the list. The Community curators are responsible for curating the dataset record and finally accept/decline the record into the Community. More than one Community can be selected.

Figure 9: Select a community from the list.

Submitting your record to a Community offers several advantages -- such as increasing the visibility and impact of your research. It improves findability, accessibility, and reusability of your dataset, and can also lead to institutional recognition and metadata improvement.

Communities in Zenodo

Read more about how to submit to a Community and how to create a Community in Zenodo submit to community1.

docs.title: 2. How to publish your data in Zenodo
docs.text:
You can only delete an unpublished record. Published records cannot be deleted except under special circumstances. You can save the dataset draft and review it before finally clicking the "Publish" button to make it publicly accessible. Make sure you have followed the Visibility option check correctly for the data files access.

Figure 10: Publish record.

What can you change after publishing?

Once your record is published, not everything works the same way:

  • Metadata (title, creators, description, licence, etc.) — can be edited directly at any time without creating a new version.
  • Data files (adding, removing, or modifying files) — requires creating a new version of the record. This generates a new DOI for the updated version.

New versions are linked to all previous versions — so if someone has cited or saved an earlier DOI, it still works and points to that specific version. Zenodo also always provides a link to the most recent version, so users can find the latest update.

See Zenodo — How to manage versions2 for step-by-step instructions.

Your dataset is now live in Zenodo!

Congratulations — your dataset has a permanent DOI and is now openly available, citable, and searchable worldwide. You have made your research reusable for others!

Share your DOI with us at data@aimms.vu.nl — we would love to feature it as an example in our growing documentation.

Further reading

Zenodo Help Documentation Zenodo — Submit to a Community Zenodo — How to manage versions

  1. Zenodo | Documentation — Submit to community: https://help.zenodo.org/docs/share/submit-to-community/ ↩

  2. Zenodo | Documentation — Manage versions: https://help.zenodo.org/docs/deposit/manage-versions/ ↩

docs.title: Getting Started with Zenodo
docs.text:
Overview

This is the Getting Started page, part of Other Tools → Zenodo in the A-LIFE RDM collection.

This document covers the first steps for using Zenodo:

  • Pre-Requirements — Sign up
